inner_thoughts: Why is that teacher down the road always full when I know I teach better than him?
I had 40 students last January. Now it's 28 and I don't even know when they left.
Every time I think about marketing I just... don't know where to start.
nodes.intro_body: If any of that sounds familiar — good, it means we've talked to enough teachers to know this is real. Here are 6 things that are actually working right now to fill tuition classes in Sri Lanka.

strategies.title: Get listed where parents are actually looking
content_paragraphs: Most teachers are on one platform, maybe two. Parents search across all of them — and if you're not there, they'll never find you.
Create a profile on at least 4 of these. It takes an afternoon and costs nothing.
Every listing needs the same 6 things — subjects, levels, location, class times, qualifications, and most importantly, your results.

visual.title: Where parents search for tuition
visual.note: 60% of teachers promote on at least one. If you're not listed, parents can't find you.

visuals.text: Refresh your listings every term. Stale listings look abandoned. Updated ones with fresh results signal you're active and filling classes.

strategies.title: Run a "results wall" on Facebook
content_paragraphs: Parents pick tuition teachers based on one thing: exam results. The teachers who fill up fastest are the ones who prove it publicly.
After every major exam result release, post a "results wall" — pass rates, A-grade counts, top scorers with consent. This isn't bragging. It's the #1 thing parents look for.
Post 2–3 study tips per week in Sinhala or Tamil. That's the content parents share with each other.
Join 3–5 parent community groups on Facebook. Don't sell. Answer questions. Be the teacher whose name is already familiar when someone asks "anyone know a good maths teacher near Nugegoda?"

strategies.title: Time your push to the enrollment calendar
content_paragraphs: If you're marketing at the wrong time of year, you're wasting effort. Enrollment follows a very specific rhythm.
Start marketing in November for January enrollment. Don't wait until January — by then the best teachers are already full.
Run crash courses during August vacation when students are free all day. Price as a lump sum (LKR 8,000–15,000) instead of monthly.

strategies.title: Offer a trial class — but make it a conversion tool
content_paragraphs: Pick a topic that shows off your teaching style. At the end, hand parents a one-pager with your results, schedule, and fee structure. Collect WhatsApp numbers.
Then — this is where most teachers drop the ball — follow up within 2 days.
That follow-up converts more students than the trial class itself. Two days. Not a week. Two days.

visual.label: Example message
visual.text: Hi Mrs. Perera, Kavinda did well in the trial class. We have 3 seats left in the Thursday batch. Want me to hold one?

strategies.title: Make it stupidly easy for parents to refer you
content_paragraphs: Word of mouth is still #1 — especially outside Colombo. But most teachers leave it to chance.
After every positive result, send this:
You're not being pushy. You're giving a happy parent permission to recommend you — with specific details to pass along.
Time these asks to right after results come out. That's when parents are happiest.

visual.label: Example message
visual.text: Really happy with Nadeesha's improvement this term! If you know any parents looking for O/L maths tuition, I have a few spots open in the Saturday batch.

strategies.title: Go where the students physically are
content_paragraphs: Print an A4 flyer with one headline result ("92% O/L pass rate 2025"), your subjects, class times, and phone number.
Place at school gates 2 weeks before January term starts and before August crash course season.
Cost: LKR 200–500 for printing. That's it.

visual.text: Schools with unfilled teaching positions are your highest-conversion spots. The national teacher absenteeism rate is 15.9% — parents near those schools are desperate for supplementary teaching.

inner_thoughts: I lost 8 students this term and I still don't know why most of them left — they just stopped showing up.
A mother called to say her daughter is switching to another teacher. I didn't even know she was unhappy.
After O/L results last March, half my batch disappeared. That hole took 3 months to fill.
nodes.intro_body: Losing students is expensive — not just in fees, but in the time it takes to replace them. Most drop-offs are preventable once you know the early signals. Here's what works.

strategies.title: Track the trend, not just the score
content_paragraphs: A parent seeing their child go from 45 to 62 to 71 over three tests won't leave — they can see the trajectory. A parent seeing three isolated scores, none of them explained, starts to wonder.
Keep a monthly test score column for every student. The number matters less than the direction.
The teachers who retain students longest aren't the ones with the highest pass rates. They're the ones who can show a parent a graph heading upward.

strategies.title: Make the parent feel like a partner, not a customer
content_paragraphs: At primary level, the parent's relationship with you matters as much as the student's. At O/L level, both matter equally. Send a short WhatsApp message once a month — not a full report, just a note.
Two sentences is enough: what the student did well this month, and what you're working on together next month.
That single message does more for retention than any results poster.

visual.label: Example monthly update
visual.text: Hi Mrs. Fernando, Kavinda did well in last week's test — 74, up from 68. He's solid on algebra, still working on graph problems. We're focusing on those this week.

strategies.title: Talk about money before it becomes a problem
content_paragraphs: The number-one reason students leave is financial pressure — but most families don't say that directly. They just stop coming.

Create two fee tiers: standard and reduced. Communicate at enrollment that you have a limited number of reduced-fee spots for students who commit to attending consistently. That gives struggling families a way to stay without the shame of asking.
You won't save every student. But you'll save more than you're saving now.

strategies.title: Plan for the post-exam cliff before it hits
content_paragraphs: After O/L and A/L exams, a predictable wave of students leaves. This isn't personal — it's structural. The teachers who recover fastest are the ones who already started recruiting the next cohort.
Start your January recruitment campaign in November — when current exam results are fresh and new parents are actively evaluating teachers for the coming year.
Run a free "exam results review" session right after results come out. It attracts next year's students and retains borderline ones who want to improve.

strategies.title: Catch drop-off before it happens
content_paragraphs: Two absences in a row is a signal. Homework consistently not done is a signal. A student going quiet in class is a signal. These things happen before a parent makes the call to leave.
After a second missed class with no message, send a check-in. Not a complaint — a genuine check-in.
That message costs 30 seconds. Keeping the student is worth months of fees.

visual.label: Example check-in message
visual.text: Hi Mrs. Kumari, just checking in — Dinesh missed Thursday. Is everything okay? We're covering exam-style questions this month and I'd hate for him to miss it.

strategies.title: Give your current students something competitors don't
content_paragraphs: Competing teachers are constantly available at lower prices. Your best defense is value that's hard to compare.

Free revision sessions in the 6 weeks before the exam. An exam technique workshop the week before results. A results-review session the day results come out. These cost you 2–3 hours and make parents feel they're in the best place.
Students who feel looked after don't switch. Students who feel like a number do.

next.label: I can't grow beyond where I am

nodes.pain_point: I can't grow beyond where I am
inner_thoughts: I teach 6 days a week already. I don't know how to fit even one more student without something breaking.
Every time I think about hiring someone, I get scared they'll ruin the reputation I spent years building.
I spend more time chasing fees and sending messages than I spend actually teaching.
nodes.intro_body: Growth stalls for specific, identifiable reasons — not because you've hit your natural limit. Here's how to find your actual bottleneck and break through it.

strategies.title: Name your actual bottleneck — it's probably not what you think
content_paragraphs: Most teachers say "I'm too busy" when what they mean is "I spend 8–12 hours a week on things that aren't teaching." The actual bottleneck is usually admin, not teaching capacity.
Track exactly what you do for one week before you try anything else. Teaching time, marking, fee-chasing, printing, WhatsApp replies — everything.
Most teachers are shocked to find they're effectively working two jobs: teacher and unpaid administrator.

strategies.title: The math on moving from home to a hall
content_paragraphs: A home-based class of 25 students at LKR 3,000/month generates LKR 75,000. A hall at LKR 25,000/month with 45 students at the same rate generates LKR 135,000 — LKR 60,000 more after rent.
The hall pays for itself once you fill 9 new students. If your waiting list already has 9+ names, the hall is money on the table.
Do the arithmetic for your own numbers before deciding. The question is never "can I afford the hall?" — it's "how many new students do I need to cover it?"

strategies.title: Add an online arm without losing your quality
content_paragraphs: Teaching 30 students physically and 20 online simultaneously with the same Zoom session is technically straightforward. The same lesson, two channels.

Price online at 60–70% of your physical rate — online students miss the in-person attention. Even at 60%, adding 20 online students adds LKR 36,000–60,000/month to your revenue without renting a bigger hall.
A teacher in Kandy can reach Colombo parents this way. The 30% of students without reliable internet still need your physical class — online supplements, it doesn't replace.

strategies.title: Hire admin before you hire teaching help
content_paragraphs: The fear of hiring is usually about quality — you don't want someone teaching your students badly. But admin help has no quality risk.
At 100+ students, a part-time admin person (3–4 hours/day, LKR 20,000–25,000/month) handles fee collection, attendance records, and parent WhatsApps. That frees 8–12 hours per week of your time.
The cost is less than 7% of a 100-student monthly revenue at average rates. The return is the time you need to grow.

strategies.title: Use crash courses to test scaling without commitment
content_paragraphs: A crash course is a finite product. You sell it, deliver it, and it ends. No long-term commitment from either side.
Run a 6-week O/L exam prep crash course during August vacation for LKR 10,000–15,000 per student. 30 students = LKR 300,000–450,000 in 6 weeks.
If it works, you've added substantial revenue and tested a new student base. If it doesn't fill, you've learned something at zero ongoing cost.

strategies.title: Kill your three biggest admin time sinks
content_paragraphs: Fee chasing (2–4 hours/week), parent communication (2–3 hours/week), and attendance tracking (1–2 hours/week) together consume 5–9 hours every week.
That's 20–36 hours per month — equivalent to one full teaching day per week, unpaid. Automating these three things gives back that time immediately.
The teachers who grow fastest aren't working harder. They've stopped doing the things a system could do for them.

nodes.pain_point: I'm too dependent on word of mouth
inner_thoughts: My three best-referring parents moved their kids to university this year. Suddenly I have no pipeline.
I keep telling myself I'll set up a Facebook page next week. That was 4 months ago.
If the O/L results don't come out well this year, I have no backup plan for enrollment.
nodes.intro_body: Word of mouth is a gift. But when it's your only channel, one bad term can unravel years of work. Here's how to build a second engine — one that keeps working even when referrals dry up.

strategies.title: Directory presence is your foundation, not Facebook
content_paragraphs: 60% of teachers already promote on at least one directory. If your profile on Iskolaya, Panthi, Mytutor, and Advice isn't current, you're invisible to parents who are actively searching right now.
Directories don't require ongoing posting. Set them up once, update after each result season.
Word of mouth brings people who already know your name. Directories bring the ones who don't know you exist yet.

visual.title: Where parents search for tuition
visual.note: If referrals dry up and you have no listings, parents who don't know you personally cannot find you.

strategies.title: Turn Facebook from a thing you mean to do into a thing that works
content_paragraphs: Most teachers post when they remember and wonder why nothing happens. The answer isn't more inspiration — it's a formula.

3 posts per week: a study tip in Sinhala/Tamil on Monday, a results or student story on Wednesday, class logistics or an exam date reminder on Friday. Post at 7pm when parents are scrolling after work.
After 90 days of this, parents in your area recognize your name. After 6 months, they recommend you to other parents unprompted — and those recommendations don't require a personal connection to you.

strategies.title: Set up a WhatsApp broadcast list — this week
content_paragraphs: A broadcast list sends a message to many parents at once, but it lands in their personal chat as if you sent it directly. It's not a group — there are no notifications from other parents, no thread to manage.
Export every current parent's number into a broadcast list. Send one update per week: exam dates, study tips, schedule changes.
This costs nothing, takes 5 minutes to set up, and keeps your name in front of every parent in your existing network.

visual.text: WhatsApp groups create noise. Broadcast lists create presence. When parents see your name in their personal chat every week, you stay top of mind — without them having to follow you anywhere.

strategies.title: Plant a YouTube channel as a long-term lead generator
content_paragraphs: You don't need to be a YouTube star. 10-minute subject explainers in Sinhala or Tamil — one per week — build a searchable library that works while you sleep.
A parent Googling "A/L chemistry diffusion Sri Lanka" and finding your video is a warm lead who already knows how you teach before they message you.
This is a 12-month game. In month 1 you have 4 videos. In month 12 you have 52, and new students find you through search. That's not word of mouth — that's a second engine.

strategies.title: Partner with schools where teachers are missing
content_paragraphs: Sri Lanka's national teacher absenteeism rate is 15.9%. Parents near government schools with chronically absent teachers are actively searching for supplementary teaching — not by choice, but because there's no alternative.
Identify the 2–3 schools nearest to you with a known reputation for absent subject teachers. Put your flyers near those schools specifically.
These parents are your most motivated prospects. They're not comparison shopping — they need you.

cards.desc: University students who attended A/L tuition

strategies.title: Engage where parents are already talking
content_paragraphs: Every area has Facebook community groups and school parent groups where parents ask each other for recommendations. Join 5 of them. Answer questions about O/L preparation, exam dates, study strategies — not as advertising, as a teacher being helpful.
When someone eventually asks "does anyone know a good chemistry teacher near Kandana?" — your name will already be familiar.
You're not selling. You're building familiarity. Familiarity converts when the moment arrives.
